summary: Lead with "Authorization checks for the affected operations" (critical), then define and enforce the contract first. 3 test suggestions, 2 fix steps.

suggestions.title: Authorization checks for the affected operations
suggestions.rationale: Authentication is not authorization; each operation must verify the caller may perform it on that resource.

draft.description: Given a caller without permission for the target resource, when the operation is attempted, then it is denied and audited.

suggestions.title: Input validation at the trust boundary
suggestions.rationale: Every externally reachable input needs validation tests: type, range, size, and encoding.

draft.description: Given malformed, oversized, and hostile inputs at the boundary, when they are submitted, then each is rejected with a safe error and no side effects.

suggestions.title: Abuse-case scenarios
suggestions.rationale: Beyond single requests: replay, enumeration, and rate abuse are how the surface actually gets attacked.

draft.description: Given scripted abuse patterns (replay, enumeration, burst rates), when they run against the surface, then limits and protections engage as documented.

steps.title: Define the validation and authorization contract
steps.description: Write down what is accepted, who may do what, and what every rejection looks like — before code.

steps.title: Enforce the contract at the boundary
steps.description: Implement validation and authorization exactly where untrusted data enters, with tests per contract clause.

risks.description: Tightening validation can break existing legitimate callers; stage the rollout and monitor rejections.

fixPolicy.rollback: Relax to log-only enforcement if legitimate traffic is rejected, then re-tighten with corrected rules.

evidence.detail: Caller requested security: Cc workload authorization: sender audience action resource payload proof expiry revocation replay and local browser guards
